etymologies.etymologyHTML: Borrowed from Middle French condenser, from Latin condēnsō.

definitions.definition: (transitive) To concentrate toward the essence by making more close, compact, or dense, thereby decreasing size or volume.

quote.citation: 1667, John Milton, “Book I”, in Paradise Lost. […], London:  […]  [Samuel Simmons], and are to be sold by Peter Parker […]; [a]nd by Robert Boulter […]; [a]nd Matthias Walker, […], →OCLC; republished as Paradise Lost in Ten Books: […], London: Basil Montagu Pickering […], 1873, →OCLC:
quote.text: In what shape they choose,  Dilated or condensed, bright or obscure.

quote.citation: 1856, John Lothrop Motley, The Rise of the Dutch Republic. A History. […], volume (please specify |volume=I to III), New York, N.Y.: Harper & Brothers, […], →OCLC:
quote.text: The secret course pursued both at Brussels and at Madrid may be condensed into the usual formula, dissimulation, procrastination, and again dissimulation.

definitions.definition: (transitive, chemistry) To transform from a gaseous state into a liquid state via condensation.
(intransitive, chemistry) To be transformed from a gaseous state into a liquid state.

quote.citation: 1692, Richard Bentley, [A Confutation of Atheism] (please specify the sermon), London: [Thomas Parkhurst; Henry Mortlock], published 1692–1693:
quote.text: The huge condense bodies of planets.
